> The boxplot for credit score also indicates the presence of outliers, as there are points that lie outside the whiskers of the boxplot.

Handling Outliers

# Applying IQR method to remove outliers from annual_spending
Q1 <- quantile(data$annual_spending, 0.25)
Q3 <- quantile(data$annual_spending, 0.75)
IQR <- Q3 - Q1

lower_bound <- Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
data_cleaned <- data %>%
  filter(annual_spending >= lower_bound & annual_spending <= upper_bound)
# Applying IQR method to remove outliers from credit_score
Q1_cs <- quantile(data$credit_score, 0.25)
Q3_cs <- quantile(data$credit_score, 0.75)
IQR_cs <- Q3_cs - Q1_cs

lower_bound_cs <- Q1_cs - 1.5 * IQR_cs
upper_bound_cs <- Q3_cs + 1.5 * IQR_cs
data_cleaned <- data_cleaned %>%
  filter(credit_score >= lower_bound_cs & credit_score <= upper_bound_cs)

Visualize after removing outliers

boxplot(data_cleaned$credit_score, main = "Boxplot of Credit Score (Cleaned Data)", ylab = "Credit Score")

# Boxplot of cleaned data
boxplot(data_cleaned$annual_spending, main = "Boxplot of Annual Spending (Cleaned Data)", ylab = "Annual Spending")

Phase 3: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Univariate Analysis

# Histogram for annual_spending
ggplot(encoded_data, aes(x = annual_spending)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 500, fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Annual Spending", x = "Annual Spending", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation: The histogram of annual spending shows a right-skewed distribution, indicating that most customers have lower annual spending, while a smaller number of customers have higher annual spending.

# Density plot for credit_score
ggplot(encoded_data, aes(x = credit_score)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Density Plot of Credit Score", x = "Credit Score", y = "Density") +
  theme_bw()

Interpretation: The density plot of credit score shows a unimodal distribution, with most customers having credit scores around the mean, and fewer customers having very low or very high credit scores.

# Frequency table for annual_income
#table(encoded_data$annual_income)
#prop.table(table(encoded_data$annual_income))

Interpretation: The frequency table for annual income shows that the majority of customers fall within the lower income brackets, with a smaller proportion of customers in the higher income brackets. This suggests that the customer base is predominantly composed of individuals with lower to moderate annual incomes.

Multivariate Analysis

# Boxplot of Spending by Region
ggplot(data_cleaned, aes(x = region, y = annual_spending)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightgreen", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Annual Spending by Region", x = "Region", y = "Annual Spending") +
  theme_classic()

Interpretation:From the boxplot of annual spending by region above, we observe that there are no significant differences in annual spending across the different regions. The median annual spending and interquartile ranges appears to be relatively similar across all regions.However, there are some outliers in suburban and urban regions, indicating that there are a few customers with significantly higher or lower annual spending compared to the majority of customers in each region.

# Boxplot of Spending by employment_status
ggplot(data_cleaned, aes(x = employment_status, y = annual_spending)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightcoral", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Annual Spending by Employment Status", x = "Employment Status", y = "Annual Spending") +
  theme_classic()

Interpretation: The boxplot of annual spending by employment status shows that there are significant differences in annual spending across different employment statuses.Self_Employed customers tend to have higher median annual spending compared to employed,student,unemployed and retired customers. Additionally, the interquartile range for employed customers is wider, indicating greater variability in annual spending among this group. Unemployed and student customers have lower median annual spending and narrower interquartile ranges, suggesting that they generally spend less annually compared to employed customers.Also, there are some outliers in the student, employed and unemployed categories, indicating that there are a few customers with significantly higher or lower annual spending compared to the majority of customers in each employment status.

#Scatterplot of income vs credit score by churn
ggplot(data_cleaned, aes(x = annual_income, y = credit_score, color = churn)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of Annual Income vs Credit Score by Churn", x = "Annual Income", y = "Credit Score") +
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation: There is a moderate positive correlation between annual income and credit score, as customers with higher annual incomes tend to have higher credit scores. Additionally, non-churned customers generally have higher credit scores compared to churned customers, regardless of their annual income. This suggests that credit score may be a more important factor in customer retention than annual income.However,there is an overlap in the scatterplot, indicating that there are some churned customers with high credit scores and some non-churned customers with low credit scores, suggesting that income and credit score alone may not fully explain customer churn, and other factors may also play a role in customer retention.

#Scatterplot of income vs credit score by churn
ggplot(data_cleaned, aes(x = annual_income, y = credit_score, )) +
  geom_point(size = 2,color ="yellow") +
  facet_wrap(~churn) +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of Annual Income vs Credit Score by Churn", x = "Annual Income", y = "Credit Score") +
  
  theme_minimal()

Interpretation: The scatterplot shows a positive correlation between annual income and credit score for both churned and non-churned customers. However, non-churned customers generally have higher credit scores compared to churned customers across all income levels. This suggests that credit score may be a more important factor in customer retention than annual income. Additionally, there is an overlap in the scatterplot, indicating that there are some churned customers with high credit scores and some non-churned customers with low credit scores, suggesting that income and credit score alone are not strong predictors of customer churn, and other factors may also play a role in customer retention.

Interpretation: The correlation matrix and heatmap reveal several significant correlations among the numerical variables. Annual spending has a strong positive correlation with annual income (r = 0.83), indicating that customers with higher incomes tend to spend more annually. Additionally, there is a moderate positive correlation between credit score and annual spending (r = 0.63), suggesting that customers with higher spendings also tend to have better credit scores. However, there is a weak negative correlation between loyalty years and annual spending (r = -0.0028), indicating that customers who have been loyal for longer periods may spend slightly less annually. Overall, these correlations suggest that income and credit score are important factors influencing annual spending, while loyalty years have a less significant impact on spending behavior.

Confidence Intervals

conf_int <- t.test(data_cleaned$annual_spending)
print(conf_int)

    One Sample t-test

data:  data_cleaned$annual_spending
t = 164.54, df = 9850, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 14703.63 15058.19
sample estimates:
mean of x 
 14880.91
  • The mean annual spending is estimated to be approximately 14880.91 with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 14703.63 to 15058.19. The interval does not include zero,indicating statistical significance at the 5% level. In addition, the confidence interval is relatively narrow, suggesting a precise estimate of the mean annual spending for the customer base. This information can be valuable for business decision-making and strategic planning related to customer spending behavior.

Phase 5: Hypothesis Testing

Parametric Tests

Two-sample t-test

State the null and alternative hypotheses
  • Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no significant difference in mean annual spending between churned and non-churned customers.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is a significant difference in mean annual spending between churned and non-churned customers.

Assumptions for the two-sample t-test and A: 1. Independence: The observations in each group (churned and non-churned) are independent of each other. 2. Normality: The annual spending variable is approximately normally distributed within each group. 3. Homogeneity of Variances: The variances of annual spending are equal across the two groups.

# Two-sample t-test for annual_spending by churn
t_test_result <- t.test(annual_spending ~ churn, data = data_cleaned)
print(t_test_result)

    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  annual_spending by churn
t = 4.3965, df = 1213.2, p-value = 1.196e-05
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group No and group Yes is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  734.7357 1918.8948
sample estimates:
 mean in group No mean in group Yes 
         15013.71          13686.90

The two-sample t-test results indicate that there is a statistically significant difference in mean annual spending between churned and non-churned customers (p-value = 0.00001196). The mean annual spending for non-churned customers is higher than that of churned customers, suggesting that customers who do not churn tend to spend more annually compared to those who do churn. This finding can provide valuable insights for customer retention strategies, as it highlights the importance of targeting non-churned customers who have higher spending potential.

ANOVA with post-hoc Analysis

Assumptions for ANOVA: 1. Independence: The observations in each group (regions) are independent of each other. 2. Normality: The annual spending variable is approximately normally distributed within each group. 3. Homogeneity of Variances: The variances of annual spending are equal across the different regions.

State the null and alternative hypotheses
  • Null Hypothesis (H0): There mean annual spendingis the same across different regions.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): At least one region has a different mean annual spending compared to the others.
model_aov <- aov(annual_spending ~ region, data = data_cleaned)
summary(model_aov)
              Df    Sum Sq   Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
region         2 5.001e+08 250050644   3.105 0.0449 *
Residuals   9848 7.932e+11  80542332                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

The reults above with an F-value of 3.105 and a p-value of 0.045 indicate that there is a statistically significant difference in mean annual spending across different regions although small. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis, suggesting that regional location does have a small significant impact on customers’ annual spending behavior in this dataset.

# Effect size calculation (Eta Squared)
library(effectsize)
eta_squared_result <- eta_squared(model_aov)
print(eta_squared_result)
# Effect Size for ANOVA

Parameter |     Eta2 |       95% CI
-----------------------------------
region    | 6.30e-04 | [0.00, 1.00]

- One-sided CIs: upper bound fixed at [1.00].

The effectsize(Eta2) of 0.00063 indicates that only 0.063% of the variance in annual spending can be explained by the region variable, suggesting a very small effect size. This implies that while there is a statistically significant difference in mean annual spending across regions, the practical significance of this difference is minimal, and other factors may play a more substantial role in influencing customers’ annual spending behavior.

# Post-hoc analysis using Tukey's HSD test
tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(model_aov)
print(tukey_result)

From the Tukey’s HSD test results, we can see that there is no statistically significant difference in mean annual spending between any pair of regions, as all p-values are greater than 0.05. This suggests that while the ANOVA indicated a significant difference across regions, the post-hoc analysis does not identify any specific pairs of regions that differ significantly from each other in terms of annual spending. Non-Parametric Tests

Mann-Whitney U Test

Assumptions for Mann-Whitney U Test: 1. Independence: The observations in each group (marital statuses) are independent of each other. 2. Ordinal or Continuous Data: The dependent variable (annual spending) should be measured at an ordinal or continuous level. 3. Non-Normal Distribution: The Mann-Whitney U test does not assume normality of the data, making it suitable for non-normally distributed data or when the sample size is small.

State the null and alternative hypotheses
  • Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no significant difference in the median annual spending between different marital statuses since the distibution of the two groups is identical.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is a significant difference in the median annual spending between different marital statuses since the distribution of the two groups is not identical.
# Mann-Whitney U test for annual_spending by churn
mann_whitney_result <- wilcox.test(annual_spending ~ marital_status, data = data_cleaned)
print(mann_whitney_result)

    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  annual_spending by marital_status
W = 11265850, p-value = 0.3673
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0

The results with a p-value of 0.3673 indicate that there is no statistically significant difference in median annual spending between different marital statuses. Therefore, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, suggesting that marital status does not have a significant impact on customers’ annual spending behavior in this dataset.

Kruskal-Wallis Test

Assumptions for Kruskal-Wallis Test: 1. Independence: The observations in each group (regions) are independent of each other. 2. Ordinal or Continuous Data: The dependent variable (annual spending) should be measured at an ordinal or continuous level. 3. Non-Normal Distribution: The Kruskal-Wallis test does not assume normality of the data, making it suitable for non-normally distributed data or when the sample size is small.

State the null and alternative hypotheses
  • Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no significant difference in the median annual spending across different regions since the distribution of annual spending is identical across all regions.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is a significant difference in the median annual spending across different regions since the distribution of annual spending is not identical across all regions.
# Kruskal-Wallis test for annual_spending by region
kruskal_result <- kruskal.test(annual_spending ~ region, data = data_cleaned)
print(kruskal_result)

    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test

data:  annual_spending by region
Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 5.7116, df = 2, p-value = 0.05751

The results with a p-value of 0.0575 indicate that there is no statistically significant difference in median annual spending across different regions at the 5% significance level. Therefore, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, suggesting that regional location does not have a significant impact on customers’ annual spending behavior in this dataset.

Chi-Square Test for Categorical Variables

Assumptions for Chi-Square Test: 1. Independence: The observations in the contingency table are independent of each other. 2. Expected Frequency: The expected frequency for each cell in the contingency table should be at least 5 to ensure the validity of the test. 3. Categorical Variables: Both variables being analyzed should be categorical in nature. 4.Sufficient Sample Size: The sample size should be sufficiently large to provide reliable results, typically with at least 20 observations per cell in the contingency table.

State the null and alternative hypotheses
  • Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no association between customer churn and region, meaning that the distribution of churn is the same across all regions.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is an association between customer churn and region, meaning that the distribution of churn differs across regions.
# Create contingency table for churn and region
contingency_table <- table(data_cleaned$churn, data_cleaned$region)
contingency_table
     
      Rural Suburban Urban
  No   1818     2632  4415
  Yes   189      293   504
# Perform Chi-Square test
chi_square_result <- chisq.test(contingency_table)
print(chi_square_result)

    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  contingency_table
X-squared = 1.0877, df = 2, p-value = 0.5805

The results above with a p-value of 0.5805 indicate that there is no statistically significant association between customer churn and region. Therefore, we fail to reject the null hypothesis, suggesting that the distribution of churn is similar across all regions in this dataset. This implies that regional location does not have a significant impact on customer churn behavior.

Phase 6 :Regression Modelling

Simple Linear Regression

State the null and alternative hypotheses
  • Null Hypothesis (H0): There is no statistically significant effect of annual income on annual spending, meaning that the slope of the regression line is equal to zero.
  • Alternative Hypothesis (H1): There is a statistically significant effect of annual income on annual spending, meaning that the slope of the regression line is not equal to zero.
# Simple linear regression for annual_spending by annual_income
model1 <- lm(annual_spending ~ annual_income, data = encoded_data)

The Equation of the SLR Model

\[ \hat{AnnualSpending} =805.4 + 0.3285 \times AnnualIncome \] Interpretation: The simple linear regression model indicates that for every one unit increase in annual income, the annual spending is expected to increase by approximately 0.3285 units, holding all else constant. The intercept of 805.4 represents the estimated annual spending when annual income is zero, although this may not be a meaningful value in practice. The model is statistically significant (p-value = 2e-16), suggesting that annual income is a significant predictor of annual spending in this dataset. However, the R-squared value of 0.6827 indicates that approximately 68.27% of the variance in annual spending can be explained by annual income while the adjusted R-squared value of 0.6827 suggests that the model has a good fit to the data, accounting for the number of predictors included in the model. Overall, this simple linear regression model provides valuable insights into the relationship between annual income and annual spending among customers in this dataset.
